waypoints.name: Killen Creek Trailhead
waypoints.directions: Reached on Forest Roads 23, 21 and 2329 from the Randle or Trout Lake side. FR-2329 holds snow well into early summer, so check the road before committing — parties blocked short of the trailhead have had to walk or bushwhack an extra mile or more of road and forest to reach it.

waypoints.name: High Camp Trail Junction
waypoints.directions: Follow Killen Creek Trail #113 up through subalpine forest and meadow for about three miles to the Pacific Crest Trail, and cross straight over onto the High Camp Trail. Killen Creek, crossed low on the trail, is the last dependable running water; everything above is melted snow. The tread thins out above treeline and is easy to lose in the dark or a whiteout, so note landmarks on the way up or carry a track.

waypoints.name: High Camp
waypoints.directions: Another mile on the High Camp Trail ends it at the edge of the Adams Glacier's lateral moraine. Sheltered bivy sites sit slightly higher, in a shallow snow gully just left of the moraine, and more camping is scattered across the benches above that.

waypoints.name: Adams Glacier Base
waypoints.directions: A patchy path runs past the upper camping area and up moraine and snow to the glacier toe, where parties rope up. Judge the timing generously — the volcano's scale flattens distance out and this leg routinely runs two hours. The point of the very early start is to be through the icefall before the sun starts working on it.

waypoints.name: Mount Adams Summit
waypoints.directions: The usual line takes the right-hand side of the glacier for roughly the first two-thirds, threading ice steps and serac lanes, then cuts back left high up onto the unbroken snow of the summit plateau. Which side of the upper icefall goes changes from year to year, and the left-hand option has been found far steeper than the grade suggests — sustained 55 to 65 degrees rather than moderate — so look at it in daylight from below before committing. The crossing beneath the ice cliffs is the stretch to move through fastest, on thin bridges and with backtracking common. Above the icefall the angle eases and two or three false summits stand between you and the true one, so keep navigating rather than trusting the first high point.

gear: Two ice tools — sustained 50-55° ice/snow with sections to ~65°
3-4 long ice screws for the steeper mid-route ice (some parties carry more, up to 6-8, depending on year/season)
3-4 pickets, distributed through the rope team, for running belays and crevasse-rescue anchors
Crevasse-rescue kit (prussiks) — the route climbs an actual icefall/glacier, not just a snowfield
Rope for the team — most parties simul-climb with running protection rather than pitching the whole route

approach_variants.name: Cold Springs trailhead and the Lunch Counter
approach_variants.notes:
From Trout Lake, drive north on Mt Adams Road to the Forest Road 23 junction, bear right about a mile to the signed FR 80 turn for South Climb, then FR 80 for 3.7 miles to FR 8040, and FR 8040 for 8.1 miles — steep, narrow, sharp switchbacks, no RVs or trailers — to the South Climb / Cold Springs trailhead at 5,600 ft.

Permits: a Cascade Volcano Pass is required to travel above 7,000 ft in the Mount Adams Wilderness during the summer season (June 1 to September 30 per the Forest Service), and a free wilderness permit is needed for the trailhead. Both can be self-issued at the trailhead, or the volcano pass can be obtained from the Mount Adams Ranger Station in Trout Lake or by mail. Weekend and weekday rates differ and an annual option exists.

The trail begins on an old roadbed through burn scar, enters subalpine forest and meadow, crosses the Round-the-Mountain Trail and the PCT, then climbs Crescent Ridge toward the snowfields. In early season there is often no trail at all — just a snow slope leading out of the parking lot. Above the Crescent Glacier the way is meandering snowfields to the Lunch Counter.

The Lunch Counter (roughly 9,250–9,400 ft) is the standard camp: a broad rocky bench with hand-built rock windbreaks. Water is snowmelt. This is a route where the crowd itself is a factor — it is the most-climbed line on the mountain and the bench fills on summer weekends.
approach_variants.season: Late May through September; earlier in the season the whole route is a snow climb from the parking lot
hazards: Rockfall and soft-snow postholing on the Crescent Glacier slopes in warm afternoons
Whiteout on the featureless snowfields between Crescent Glacier and the Lunch Counter
Turning around at Piker's Peak believing it is the summit
Uncontrolled glissading — the standard descent line has caused injuries
No water above the Lunch Counter; snowmelt only
Sharp switchbacks and rough surface on FR 8040, and snow blocking it early in the season
approach_variants.baseFinding:
There is no bergschrund and no ice step on this route, so the question 'where does the climbing start' has two answers, and the second one is the one that turns people around short of the top.

The first: the Lunch Counter is the transition. You are there when the meandering snowfields end at a broad, flat, rocky bench with rock walls built on it and the South Spur rising directly above as one continuous slope. Above the bench there is no more wandering — it is 2,400 ft of steepening snow on a bearing of roughly north-northeast.

The second, and the important one: what you top out on is NOT the summit. The rounded high point at 11,644 ft is Piker's Peak, the false summit. The test is unmistakable if you know to look for it — the ground ahead of you FLATTENS into a broad saddle and plateau, and a separate dome rises about 600 ft beyond it to the north. If the slope has stopped and the true top is still visibly above and away from you, you are on Piker's. Parties turn around here every season believing they have finished.

Negative marker on the way up: if you are scrambling on a rocky crest rather than kicking steps on snow, you have drifted onto Suksdorf Ridge. That is a legitimate alternative when the snow is soft, but when the snow is firm it is the slower choice, and in a whiteout it is the wrong handrail.

before.beta: The route climbs the north-facing slope between the Adams Glacier (on climber's right) and the Northwest Ridge crest (on climber's left, avoided for its poor rock), gaining access below the glacier to avoid crevasses/moats, then following steepening 40-45 degree neve past a narrow rock-band pinch to the ridge crest near 10,000 ft and on to the summit.

approach_variants.name: Killen Creek and High Camp, then the north-facing slope below the Adams Glacier terminus
approach_variants.notes:
Forest roads from the Takhlakh Lake area to the Killen Creek trailhead, then Killen Creek Trail #113 to the PCT junction and High Camp Trail #10 to the meadow camp at about 6,900 ft.

From camp, gain the north-facing slope that sits between the Adams Glacier and the crest of the Northwest Ridge. The line deliberately gains access BELOW the Adams Glacier terminus to avoid its crevasses and moats, then follows steepening 40 to 45 degree neve past a narrow rock-band pinch to the ridge crest near 10,000 ft and on to the summit.

The ridge crest itself is avoided on purpose: the rock on it is poor.

Descent is along the North Ridge back to the Adams Glacier basin high camp, or in ski conditions the route itself can be reversed, threading the same rock-band pinch.
hazards: A terrain trap between cliff bands with limited escape once committed mid-route
A narrow rock-band pinch that tightens to AI2-3 in low-snow years
Crevasse and moat hazard where the route gains ground below the Adams Glacier terminus
Poor rock on the adjacent ridge crest, which is why the line avoids it
Sustained 40-45 degree neve with a running belay the only practical protection
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS ROUTE IS THE GROUND BETWEEN TWO THINGS, SO THE TEST IS THAT YOU HAVE ONE ON EACH SIDE.

AS YOU CLIMB, THE ADAMS GLACIER SHOULD BE ON YOUR RIGHT AND THE CREST OF THE NORTHWEST RIDGE ON YOUR LEFT. If both are on the same side of you, you are on one of them rather than between them, and you are not on this route.

THE ROCK IS THE NEGATIVE ON ONE SIDE, AND IT IS TACTILE, WHICH IS WHAT YOU WANT AT NIGHT: this line stays OFF the crest because the crest's rock is poor. If you are pulling on loose blocky rock instead of kicking steps in neve, you have drifted left onto the ridge.

THE CREVASSES ARE THE NEGATIVE ON THE OTHER SIDE: the route gains its ground BELOW the Adams Glacier terminus specifically so it does not have to deal with the glacier's crevasses and moats. If you are stepping across crevasses, you are too far right and on the Adams Glacier route, which is a different and harder climb.

THE POSITIVE, AND IT IS COUNTABLE: ONE CONSTRICTION. A narrow pinch through a rock band, ski-width or body-width, is the crux and the only place the route squeezes. If you have climbed a couple of thousand feet of 40 to 45 degree neve and met no constriction, the pinch is still above you and you are on route. If you met a constriction in the first rope length, you are somewhere else.

WHAT THE PINCH MEANS FOR CONDITIONS: it gets tighter in a low-snow year, which is when it becomes the AI2-3 crux rather than a step. It is also a terrain trap — you are between cliff bands there with limited escape, so decide about it from below rather than at it.

TOP-OUT CHECK: the route joins the NORTHWEST RIDGE CREST near 10,000 ft. Gaining a crest at that height is correct; gaining one much lower means you climbed onto the ridge early instead of past it.

before.bail: Below about 10,000 ft, retreat by downclimbing the neve back toward the Adams Glacier terminus; above that, escape onto the North Ridge crest once angle allows.

approach_variants.name: Killen Creek trailhead and High Camp
approach_variants.notes:
The same walk in as the Adams Glacier and the Northwest Ridge, and High Camp is the shared base for all three. Killen Creek Trail #113 from the trailhead (~4,600 ft) runs about 3.1 miles to the PCT junction at roughly 6,100 ft; cross straight over onto High Camp Trail #10 for another mile to its end at about 6,900 ft on the edge of the Adams Glacier moraine. Camping is spread between 7,000 and 7,600 ft, including a glacial lake camp near 7,650 ft.

Access is by FR 23, 21 and 2329; FR 2329 is gravel and holds snow into early summer. Killen Creek low on the trail is the last dependable water.

Permits: free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead, plus a Cascade Volcano Pass for travel above 7,000 ft in the summer season.

This is a longer and more committing day than the South Climb from a much quieter side of the mountain, and it involves more crevassed ground — roped travel and glacier skills are expected, unlike the South Spur.
approach_variants.season: June through September; a snow route early, a loose rock route once it melts out
hazards: Very loose volcanic rock the length of the ridge — helmets, and spacing between climbers
Crevassed glacier on both flanks if you leave the crest
Exposed snow travel between rock sections
Thin moraine tread above treeline, easy to lose in dark or whiteout
No running water above Killen Creek
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From High Camp the line is southeast, toward the foot of the ridge, and in clear weather you can see the whole thing from the approach — parties describe it as impossible to miss.

The recognition problem is entirely a poor-visibility one, and the test is what is under your boots. The North Ridge is the rubble-and-cinder rib that separates the Adams Glacier on its west from the Lava Glacier ground on its east. You should be on loose volcanic rock and scree, on a defined crest, with glacier falling away on BOTH sides. If you are on ice with crevasses, you have slid off the rib onto one glacier or the other, and which one tells you which way to correct.

A smooth, clean, snow-only ascent is the wrong sign on this route: it is a choss pile, and the loose rock is the confirmation rather than the complaint. Expect short easy scrambling steps low down.

The angle eases noticeably around 11,000 ft, which is the sign the ridge proper is behind you and the summit plateau ground is ahead.

hazards: Steep, sustained snow on the upper ridge with rockfall from the ridge crest
Crevasses on the Lava and Lyman glacier approaches
Cornices on the ridgeline
Remote north-side approach — long self-reliant day

weather.typical: North-facing, holds snow longer and colder than the south side
weather.probability: Not explicitly documented for this route; Cascade volcanoes commonly see afternoon convective activity in summer, as noted for the South Climb, so treat as a plausible but unverified risk here

seasonal_hazards.exposure: High - sustained steep snow on the upper ridge with rockfall from the crest as it warms, cornices along the ridgeline, and a remote, self-reliant north-side approach with no quick bailout
seasonal_hazards.crevasses: Crevasses on the Lava and Lyman glacier approaches/descent require roped travel and crevasse-rescue readiness
